lead: An op-amp with two resistors sets a precise gain. In the inverting amplifier, R₁ feeds a virtual ground and R_f returns from the output, so v_out = −(R_f/R₁)v_in. In the non-inverting amplifier, the input goes to the + terminal, so v_out = (1 + R_f/R₁)v_in and the input draws almost no current. The voltage follower is the non-inverting case with R₁ open: gain 1, very high input resistance, low output resistance. These circuits buffer sensors, set audio gain and isolate reference dividers.
prereq: You need: Chapter 6.1 for the ideal model and virtual ground, and Unit 4 for negative feedback.

blocks.text: The inverting amplifier grounds the + input and places R₁ between the source and the − input, with R_f from output to − input. Negative feedback forces the − input to the same 0 V as the + input. That point is a virtual ground: it sits at 0 V but the op-amp does not sink current there.
The input current is i = v_in/R₁. The op-amp input draws no current, so the same i must flow through R_f. The output must supply v_out = 0 − iR_f = −(R_f/R₁)v_in. The minus sign means inversion.

blocks.where: A_v is the voltage gain; R_f is the feedback resistor from output to the inverting input; R₁ is the input resistor from source to the inverting input.

items: Input resistance is exactly R₁ because the inverting node is at 0 V.
Keep R₁ above about 1 kΩ to avoid loading the source.
Choose R_f = |A_v|R₁ and keep R_f below about 1 MΩ.
For bias-current balance, add R_comp = R₁ parallel R_f from the + input to ground.

blocks.text: The non-inverting amplifier connects v_in to the + input and uses a divider: R_f from output to − input, R₁ from − input to ground. Negative feedback makes v₋ = v_in. The current in R₁ is v_in/R₁, and the same current flows in R_f because the op-amp input draws none. The output is v_out = v_in + iR_f = (1 + R_f/R₁)v_in.

blocks.where: R_f is the feedback resistor from output to the inverting input; R₁ is the resistor from the inverting input to ground; A_v is always at least 1.

blocks.text: The input resistance is set by the op-amp and is very high; the output resistance is low. The gain cannot be less than 1.

The voltage follower, also called a buffer or unity-gain amplifier, is this circuit with R₁ open and R_f = 0. Then v_out = v_in. It gives no voltage gain but gives current gain: a weak sensor can drive a heavy load, and a divider is not loaded by the next stage.

For a target non-inverting gain G, pick R₁ between about 1 kΩ and 100 kΩ, then R_f = (G − 1)R₁, keeping R_f below about 1 MΩ. For an inverting gain −G, use R_f = G R₁. Add the compensating resistor only when bias-current error matters. Cascade two stages by multiplying their gains; the sign of each stage also multiplies.

Finite open-loop gain A_OL makes the closed-loop gain slightly smaller than ideal. The fractional error is about (1 + R_f/R₁)/A_OL for both connections. A gain of 10 with A_OL = 10⁵ has about 0.011 % error; a gain of 100 has about 0.1 %. More open-loop gain buys more accuracy.

The inverting input resistance is R₁; the non-inverting input resistance is the op-amp input resistance, usually very high. Output resistance is the op-amp output resistance divided by roughly (1 + loop gain), so it is low. Stray capacitance at the inverting node causes peaking; keep R_f modest or add a small feedback capacitor. Closed-loop frequency response is covered in Unit 3.

figure.caption: The input resistor turns v_in into 20 µA into a virtual ground; R_f carries the same current from the output, giving v_out = −2 V. Notice the inverting node stays at 0 V, not at v_in.

spec.title: Inverting amplifier signal path
spec.aria: Signal path of the inverting amplifier: R₁ turns 0.2 V into 20 µA into a virtual ground, and R_f carries the same current back to set v_out = −2 V.

examples.question: An inverting amplifier uses R₁ = 10 kΩ and R_f = 100 kΩ with v_in = 0.2 V. Find the ideal gain, output and input current. Repeat for the non-inverting connection with the same resistors. For the inverting circuit, take A_OL = 10⁵ and estimate the actual gain and its percentage error.
steps: Inverting ideal gain: A_v = −R_f/R₁ = −100 kΩ / 10 kΩ = −10.
Inverting output: v_out = A_v v_in = −10 × 0.2 V = −2 V.
Input current: i = v_in/R₁ = 0.2 V / 10 kΩ = 20 µA. The same 20 µA flows in R_f.
Non-inverting gain: A_v = 1 + R_f/R₁ = 1 + 100 kΩ / 10 kΩ = 11.
Finite A_OL: loop factor is 1 + R_f/R₁ = 11, so gain ≈ −10 / (1 + 11/10⁵) = −9.9989.
examples.answer: The inverting amplifier gives gain −10 and output −2 V with 20 µA input current; the non-inverting amplifier gives gain 11 and output 2.2 V; finite A_OL lowers the inverting magnitude to 9.9989, an error of 0.011 %.
examples.check:
R1 = 10e3
Rf = 100e3
vin = 0.2
Aol = 1e5
gain_inv = -Rf / R1
vout_inv = gain_inv * vin
i_in = vin / R1
gain_non = 1 + Rf / R1
vout_non = gain_non * vin
gain_fin = -10 / (1 + 11 / Aol)
err = abs((abs(gain_fin) / abs(gain_inv) - 1) * 100)
print(gain_inv)
print(vout_inv)
print(i_in)
print(gain_non)
print(vout_non)
print(round(gain_fin, 4))
print(round(err, 4))

traps: Using R_f/R₁ for the non-inverting gain. The correct non-inverting gain is 1 + R_f/R₁; the extra 1 is the input signal itself.
Calling the inverting input a high-resistance node. The source sees R₁ to a virtual ground, so input resistance is R₁.
Dropping the minus sign in the inverting gain, or expecting a negative output from the non-inverting circuit.
Leaving R₁ in place for a voltage follower. The follower is the non-inverting case with R₁ open and R_f = 0, so gain is 1.
Choosing R_f above about 1 MΩ or R₁ below about 1 kΩ without reason; bias current, stray capacitance and source loading grow.

quiz.q: Write the ideal gain formulas for the inverting and non-inverting amplifiers.
Why is the inverting input a virtual ground, and why is it not a high-resistance input?
quiz.a: Negative feedback plus infinite open-loop gain forces v₋ = v₊ = 0 V. The source still sees R₁ from the input to that 0 V node, so the input resistance is R₁, not infinite.

quiz.q: An inverting amplifier has R₁ = 2.2 kΩ, R_f = 47 kΩ and v_in = 50 mV. Find the gain and output.
Same resistors as the previous question, but in the non-inverting connection with v_in = 50 mV. Find the gain and output.
A 1 V sensor has 10 kΩ output resistance and drives a 1 kΩ load. Compare the load voltage directly and through an ideal follower.
quiz.a: Direct: divider 1 kΩ / (10 kΩ + 1 kΩ) gives 0.0909 V. Follower input draws no current and output resistance is low, so the load gets about 1 V. The buffer prevents loading.

quiz.q: Why does finite A_OL cause a larger gain error at high closed-loop gain?
quiz.a: Error fraction ≈ (1 + R_f/R₁)/A_OL, so it grows with the designed gain. At gain 100 with A_OL = 10⁵ the error is about 0.1 %, ten times the error at gain 10.

quiz.q: Give two resistor-choice rules for a linear op-amp stage.
quiz.a: Keep R₁ above about 1 kΩ and R_f below about 1 MΩ; add a bias-current compensating resistor matched to the DC resistance at the other input.

beyond: Not for the exam. The same resistor pair is the gain-setting network in programmable gain amplifiers, ADC drivers and audio preamps. Industrial designs add a small capacitor across R_f to control the peaking named in this chapter, and they use low-tolerance resistors when gain accuracy matters. Search for op-amp transimpedance amplifier and difference amplifier resistor mismatch to continue.
